name: Throw and catch a frisbee accurately
blurb: The backhand gets you playing; the forehand flick is what makes you actually useful in a game. Accuracy comes from a flat release, not from arm strength.
gear: A 175 g ultimate disc, not a beach frisbee
An open field and a partner or a target
steps: Fix the backhand grip — thumb on top, fingers curled under the rim — and throw with a whipping wrist snap rather than a big arm swing.
Keep the disc flat at release. Tilt is what makes it curve away and nosedive.
Learn the forehand flick: two fingers inside the rim, elbow tucked, wrist snapping the disc out flat.
Practise both throws at 10 metres until they land within a body-width of your target, then step back.
Learn the two-handed pancake catch for chest-height discs and the one-handed rim catch for everything else.
Practise throwing into wind and downwind — the disc behaves completely differently.
tips: Nose-up release is the classic fault: the disc climbs, stalls and dies. Aim to release with the front edge slightly down.
Snap, do not swing. The wrist provides the spin, and spin provides the stability.
proof: Ten forehands and ten backhands at 20 metres, each catchable without your partner moving more than a step.
